verses.text: When Yahweh was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
Elijah said to Elisha, “Please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me as far as Bethel.” Elisha said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they went down to Bethel.
The sons of the prophets who were at Bethel came out to Elisha, and said to him, “Do you know that Yahweh will take away your master from your head today?” He said, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”
Elijah said to him, “Elisha, please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me to Jericho.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they came to Jericho.

The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho came near to Elisha, and said to him, “Do you know that Yahweh will take away your master from your head today?” He answered, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”
Elijah said to him, “Please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me to the Jordan.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” Then they both went on.
Fifty men of the sons of the prophets went, and stood opposite them at a distance; and they both stood by the Jordan.
Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters, and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground.
When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.”
He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be so for you; but if not, it will not be so.”
As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Elisha saw it, and he cried, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” He saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes, and tore them in two pieces.
He also took up Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and went back, and stood by the bank of the Jordan.
He took Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and struck the waters, and said, “Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?” When he also had struck the waters, they were divided apart, and Elisha went over.
When the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho over against him saw him, they said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” They came to meet him, and bowed themselves to the ground before him.

They said to him, “See now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. Perhaps Yahweh’s Spirit has taken him up, and put him on some mountain, or into some valley. He said, “Don’t send them.”
When they urged him until he was ashamed, he said, “Send them.” Therefore they sent fifty men; and they searched for three days, but didn’t find him.
They came back to him, while he stayed at Jericho; and he said to them, “Didn’t I tell you, ‘Don’t go?’”
The men of the city said to Elisha, “Behold, please, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees; but the water is bad, and the land is barren.”
He said, “Bring me a new jar, and put salt in it.” Then they brought it to him.
He went out to the spring of the waters, and threw salt into it, and said, “Yahweh says, ‘I have healed these waters. There shall not be from there any more death or barren wasteland.’”
So the waters were healed to this day, according to Elisha’s word which he spoke.
He went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, some youths came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!”
He looked behind him and saw them, and cursed them in Yahweh’s name. Then two female bears came out of the woods, and mauled forty-two of those youths.
He went from there to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.

footnotes.content: The story begins with Yahweh's intention—He will take Elijah to heaven—and with it, Elisha's faithful choosing: to stay close. Notice Elijah doesn't force this. He offers his servant a chance to turn back, as if to say, 'You can let me go.' But Elisha won't. That's the kind of loyalty Jesus calls us to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bethel means 'house of God'—a place where Jacob once dreamed of heaven. Elijah speaks as if testing Elisha; Elisha answers with a solemn oath ('as Yahweh lives, as your soul lives'). He will not abandon his master. That's the kind of 'follow me' covenant Jesus makes with each of us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophets already know what's happening—the Spirit moves freely among them. But Elisha keeps his peace. There's wisdom in not speaking what everyone already feels. Sometimes the deepest loyalty is shown by standing quiet beside the one we love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah tries again to send Elisha away. Three times—each station taking them closer to the Jordan where they will part. Each time, Elisha refuses. Do you see how he mirrors what Christ asks of us: 'Will you follow me to the end, even when I don't force you?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again, the prophets speak what they know. Again, Elisha says nothing. His answer lies in his feet—in his staying. Sometimes faithfulness is less about words and more about the simple choice to keep walking beside the one God has called us to serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jordan—the river of crossing, where God's people pass from wilderness to promise. Elisha refuses to wait, to stay safe on the shore. He goes with Elijah all the way to the crossing. It's a picture of what Jesus does for us at the water's edge between this life and the next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifty prophets watch from a distance. They see what's about to happen, but they cannot go where Elijah and Elisha are going. Some walks in faith we must make alone with the Lord—witnesses stand by, but the crossing is ours alone to make.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Elisha's faithfulness: how often do we follow a spiritual teacher or mentor, only to discover that true faithfulness means we must learn to walk alone with the Lord? Elijah passes the mantle; Christ asks us to pick it up ourselves and strike our own Jordan. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful for leaders who teach us not to cling to them, but to learn to hear God's voice directly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah rolls up his mantle and strikes the water—the Jordan parts. This echoes Moses parting the Red Sea, echoes Joshua crossing into Canaan. Now Elisha walks through on dry ground. The mantle will soon pass to him, but first he must cross with his master as a true disciple.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah grants Elisha one request before he's taken away. Elisha asks for a 'double portion of your spirit'—not to be greater, but to carry forward the work God has begun. It's the same spirit that calls us to ask for the Holy Spirit and the gifts we need to serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah answers with a condition: 'If you see me when I am taken from you.' Seeing requires faith and faithfulness. We cannot always see the Lord working in our lives, yet we trust anyway. Elisha's whole journey has been one long act of seeing—of faithful presence to what God is doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Suddenly, fire and horses—heaven tears open to take Elijah. A whirlwind carries him up. Elisha sees it all. In that moment, the old prophet is gone, but his God remains. That's what faith holds onto: not the leader, but the Lord behind the leader.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha cries out: 'My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!' He tears his clothes—grief is honest and whole. He watched his beloved master taken. Then silence. He knew his call was real only because his loss was real. Faithfulness ends in letting go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mantle falls. Elisha picks it up—the symbol of office, of calling. He takes it back to the Jordan's bank. He's not rushing forward yet. He stands at the threshold, holding what's been passed to him, gathering himself for what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: With Elijah's mantle, Elisha strikes the water. 'Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?' he asks aloud. The Jordan divides again. In that moment, Elisha knows: the God of Elijah is now his God too. The mantle is a symbol, but the power is in the name of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophets see Elisha crossing alone with the mantle, and they recognize: 'The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.' No ceremony, no laying on of hands—his faithful presence and that one act of faith declared him the new prophet. Character and faithfulness speak louder than any title.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They want to search for Elijah—perhaps the Spirit has set him on a mountain or valley. Elisha says, 'Don't send them.' He knows something they're beginning to learn: the Lord takes His prophets home when His work with them is done. We cannot chase what God has already released.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They press him until shame moves him to relent. Sometimes we must let others learn by searching. They take three days to learn what Elisha already knew—Elijah is gone for good. There's a kindness in letting people find their own way to hard truths.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They return, and Elisha's words are gentle: 'Didn't I tell you?' No rebuke, just the simple echo of what he already knew. A good leader doesn't mock the learning of others, even when the lesson has cost them time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The city of Jericho—the place of walls and resurrection. Its people now come with a problem: the water is bad, the land barren. They come humbly to the new prophet, as if recognizing that even in a place of remembered victory, healing must come fresh from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha asks for a jar and salt—common things. He doesn't perform a grand ritual. The power lies not in the drama but in the Lord's word spoken through a faithful prophet. Sometimes the greatest works begin with simple, humble requests.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha goes to the spring and speaks Yahweh's word: 'I have healed these waters.' Salt preserves; here it becomes a sign of healing. No death, no barrenness will come from this water anymore. Through Elisha, the Lord speaks life into a place marked by decay.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The waters were healed 'to this day'—the writer speaks of something that lasted, something still true in their present. A faithful prophet's word carries forward into the future. Our faithfulness in small moments touches generations we may never see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Youths mock Elisha: 'Go up, you baldy!' They mock his appearance, his age, his calling. A prophet is often lonely, often mocked by those who do not see. Yet Elisha walks on. There is a quiet courage in continuing to serve when others laugh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha curses them in Yahweh's name, and bears come from the woods. This is hard to read—the judgment feels swift. But remember: Elisha has been tested and proven faithful. He speaks with God's authority now. The Lord takes the mocking of His prophets seriously, yet His restraint elsewhere shows mercy still available.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha travels to Mount Carmel, where Elijah once stood, and returns to Samaria. He's no longer the servant walking behind his master. He walks the land now as the prophet himself, following the same paths, continuing the same work. Faithfulness passes the torch, and the torch still burns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
